newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel says Germany on EMU track, omits key phrase.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel says Germany on EMU track, omits key phrase.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday said recent economic data would not force Germany to abandon its budget forecasts and Bonn would still meet the fiscal targets for European monetary union.

Should economic developments endanger Germany's ability to meet the Maastricht treaty targets, Waigel said Bonn would not hesitate to take additional measures to rein in budget deficits and called for strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.
However, the affable Bavarian omitted two key phrases from his speech on issues that have caused controversy within the parties in Germany's ruling coalition government.

In the text of the speech, Waigel was to counter speculation he was softening his position on monetary union by saying: "I have not changed my view. I will oppose any weakening of the criteria, three is three," and "Convergence will determine the timetable -- for each country."
But when presenting the speech to a savings bank conference in Ludwigsburg, Waigel dropped the key phrases "three is three" and "convergence will determine the timetable".

He has insisted repeatedly that the economic entry criterion for European monetary union, which calls for a country's budget deficit to be no more than three percent, must be interpreted absolutely strictly.

But he has come under pressure in the coalition both to ease off and to tighten up on the Maastricht budget deficit target, in the face of growing worries that Germany may not be able to cut its deficits far enough.

He had already backed off calling for a precise "3.0 percent", preferring to speak only of "three percent", which some economists have interpreted as meaning Germany could live with a few points behind the decimal point.
Similarly, his insistence that the level of convergence must take precedence over the timetable for the 1999 start of EMU had been attacked by those who shun a delay in the launch.
Asked after his address why he had omitted the remarks, Waigel said. "Both the written and the spoken word are valid," he told reporters.
The treaty on European economic and monetary union states that participants must fulfil a range of fiscal targets in 1997 and demonstrate lasting fiscal stability.
Based on economic data from this year, the European Union will determine early next year which countries meet the targets and qualify for entry into monetary union.

While most countries already meet some of the targets such as inflation below three percent, most are having difficulties meeting the cap on public debt of 60 percent of gross domestic product and on budget deficits of three percent of GDP.

Germany failed last year to meet the targets and runs the risk of missing the goals again this year, which has fuelled speculation that either EMU will be weakened or it will be delayed because it would be unthinkable without Germany.

"The yardstick is the lasting fulfilment of the determined criteria. The German government considers it indispensible that there is a strict and narrow interpretation of the treaty regulations," Waigel said.

"Germany will fulfil the criteria," he added. "Even current developments give no cause to veer from these forecasts. But should there still be a need to act, we will not hesitate to do what is necessary."

Waigel also took time to explain that Germany's austerity measures were not only aimed at meeting the Maastricht targets, but that budget savings were needed to get Europe's biggest economy back in shape for global competition.
But without the timely introduction of the euro, as the new currency will be called, market pressures could develop that could wipe out the progress that Germany has made in this direction.
"If the euro does not come, the mark will come under upward pressure. The export economy will suffer, jobs will be lost and public budgets will be hit," Waigel warned.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150
